newsitem.title: USA: Late push leads to superb US 10-yr index note sale.
newsitem.headline: Late push leads to superb US 10-yr index note sale.

text.p: The new index-linked 10-year note turned into the U.S. Treasury's version of "The Little Engine That Could," as Wednesday's auction turned out far better than just about everyone in the market had imgained.
Treasury sold $7.0 billion of the new inflation protected 10-year notes at a 3-3/8 percent coupon and awarded at a rate of 3.449 percent, well below all estimations.

Just prior to the 1300 EST/1800 GMT bidding deadline, analysts polled by Reuters predicted a rate of 3.51 to 3.52 percent. Others had braced for rates of 3.60 percent and up, given recent negative sentiment toward the new issues.
"We saw overwhelming demand at the last minute," said Scott Graham, a trader at Prudential Securities Inc.
Players were mum on who actually bought the new notes.
Graham speculated they were gobbled up by just three or four accounts. Earlier in the week he expressed interest in the new issues, noting that at 3.50 percent or above they represented good value.
"We anticipated buying them at 3.50-3.55 percent, not 3.45 percent," Graham said, declining to say if he bought any.
The bid-to-cover ratio of 5.31 was said to have been excellent, but the $157 million in non-competitive bids was deemed low, suggesting the sale was mostly dealer-driven.

"On the surface, it looks good," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "But since it is a new instrument, you can't compare it to anything. No doubt it went better than anyone envisioned. It alleviated concerns how (the new notes) would be received."
One head trader at a U.S.-based primary dealership said he saw good value in the index-linked 10-year notes as low as 3.30 percent. "So, we have another 10 basis points to go."
The when-issued 10-year note's rate fell following the auction to around 3.40 percent and the successful auction lifted Treasury prices across the curve.

Since the Treasury's announcement in 1996 that it planned to sell inflation-protected bonds, the concept has come under much criticsm. Much of it centered on players not believing index-linked bonds were as good an investment as traditional Treasuries, which already have an inflation premium priced in.
In recent days, however, some traders said they noticed some interest. But as late as midday Wednesday, players were unsure what the outcome of the auction would be.
Earlier on Wednesday, the when-issued 10-year note had traded as high as 3.54 percent.
"But as people were sniffing around, they started liking them and it snowballed," the head trader said. "We had outstanding late demand."
One known purchaser was the Federal Reserve, which bought $350 million of the notes for its own account.
Also, there has been market talk of heavy bidding by Asian funds and by a U.S. west coast bond fund.
"Will we get the same performance three months from now?" asked Flanagan. "It is hard to come up with an answer."
